title: Consumer Protection and Financial Inclusion
summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess product governance, fair value, disclosure, vulnerable customer treatment, complaints and financial inclusion.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to protect consumers and investors across all financial sectors: assessing product governance and fair value, disclosure, vulnerable customer treatment, complaints and access to financial services.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors a structured, outcomes-focused approach to consumer and investor protection that applies across banking, insurance, investment and payments. Participants leave able to assess whether firms deliver fair outcomes in practice, recognise signs of consumer harm and exclusion, and turn analysis into proportionate supervisory action.
sections.What It Covers: Consumer protection principles, product governance, fair value, disclosure and consumer understanding, vulnerable customers, complaints handling and redress, issuer disclosure, financial inclusion and de-risking, outcomes monitoring, and emerging digital harms.
Intended Audience: Conduct and consumer protection supervisors and inspectors across all sectors
Policy staff working on consumer protection, disclosure or financial inclusion
Senior managers setting the authority's consumer protection priorities
Learning Objectives: Explain the principles and international standards underpinning consumer and investor protection
Assess product governance, fair value and disclosure from the consumer's perspective
Evaluate how firms identify and treat vulnerable customers and handle complaints
Apply the principles of full, accurate and timely issuer disclosure to supervisory review
Balance financial inclusion against financial crime and prudential objectives
Use consumer outcomes data to prioritise and justify supervisory intervention
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a practical briefing with case studies, red flags and supervisory question exercises, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of conduct or consumer-facing supervision is helpful. No specialist background is required.
Core Reading: G20/OECD High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection (2022)
World Bank, Good Practices for Financial Consumer Protection (2017)
CPMI and World Bank, Payment Aspects of Financial Inclusion (2016)

modules.title: Foundations of Consumer Protection Supervision
modules.summary: Why consumer and investor protection matters to supervisors, the international principles that underpin it, and how outcomes-based supervision differs from rules-based compliance checking.
objectives: Explain the rationale for consumer and investor protection
Describe the relevant international principles and standards
Distinguish outcomes-based from rules-based consumer supervision
syllabus: Information asymmetry, behavioural biases and consumer harm
IOSCO investor protection objective and G20/OECD consumer protection principles
Links between consumer outcomes, conduct risk and firm culture
The customer journey as a supervisory lens

modules.title: Product Governance and Target Markets
modules.summary: How firms should design, distribute and review products for a defined target market, and how supervisors test whether product governance works in practice.
objectives: Explain the product governance lifecycle from design to review
Assess target market definition and distribution strategy
Identify common product governance failures
syllabus: Product approval, target market and negative target market
Distribution chains and manufacturer versus distributor responsibilities
Ongoing product review and management information
Red flags in product governance files

modules.title: Fair Value Assessment
modules.summary: How to assess whether the price consumers pay is reasonable relative to the benefits, costs and quality they receive, and how to challenge firms' value assessments.
objectives: Apply a fair value framework to a financial product
Challenge the evidence behind a firm's value assessment
Identify pricing practices that cause foreseeable harm
syllabus: Price, benefits, costs and quality as value components
Price walking, cross-subsidy and hidden charges
Value across distribution chains and add-on products
Exercise: testing a firm's fair value assessment

modules.title: Disclosure, Communications and Consumer Understanding
modules.summary: How to evaluate whether disclosures and communications are clear, fair and not misleading, drawing on behavioural insights into how consumers actually process information.
objectives: Evaluate disclosure documents for consumer understanding
Apply behavioural insights to communications and choice architecture
Assess how firms test and monitor communication effectiveness
syllabus: Clear, fair and not misleading communications
Behavioural insights: framing, defaults and information overload
Digital journeys, dark patterns and financial promotions
Consumer testing and monitoring of disclosure effectiveness

modules.title: Identifying and Protecting Vulnerable Customers

Describe regulatory expectations for identifying vulnerable customers
Assess the adequacy of a firm's vulnerable-customer policy

Identify gaps between a firm's stated policy and its practical delivery

Vulnerability as a spectrum, not a fixed category
Regulatory expectations for identifying vulnerable customers

Facilitated discussion: how vulnerability shows up in different sectors
Exercise: map vulnerability drivers to customer scenarios
What a good vulnerable-customer policy contains
Frontline identification: training, tools, escalation routes
Tailoring products, communications and service
Common weaknesses in practice versus policy
Group exercise: review a sample vulnerable-customer policy
Role-play: a frontline interaction with a vulnerable customer
Case examples of good and poor tailored treatment
Identifying the gap between stated policy and delivery
Supervisory tools for assessing vulnerable-customer outcomes
Escalation and intervention where practice falls short
Case study: assess a firm's vulnerable-customer framework and produce supervisory conclusions
Recap: vulnerability drivers, policy assessment, practical delivery
Reinforcing the spectrum view of vulnerability
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Supervising Complaints Handling and Redress
modules.summary: How to supervise firms' complaints handling and root-cause analysis, how redress schemes operate, and how complaints data can serve as an early warning of wider harm.
objectives: Explain expectations for timely, fair complaints handling
Assess root-cause analysis and its use in remediation
Use complaints and redress data as supervisory intelligence
syllabus: The complaints process end to end and governance oversight
Root-cause analysis: from individual complaints to systemic issues

Complaints data as an early warning indicator

modules.title: Issuer Disclosure as Investor Protection
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to deepen participants' understanding of issuer disclosure as a core investor-protection mechanism, drawing on IOSCO's Principles for Issuers, and to build practical skills in assessing whether disclosure practices are full, accurate, and timely.
objectives: Explain the role of disclosure in protecting investors
Describe IOSCO's Principles for Issuers and their disclosure requirements
Assess whether disclosure is full, accurate and timely
Evaluate the quality of financial and non-financial disclosures
Identify red flags in issuer disclosure practices
Formulate supervisory conclusions on disclosure adequacy
syllabus: IOSCO's investor-protection objective and the role of disclosure
The Principles for Issuers: full, accurate and timely disclosure
Financial versus non-financial disclosure
Consequences of disclosure failures for investors and markets
Facilitated discussion: notable disclosure failures and their investor impact
Frameworks for assessing disclosure completeness and accuracy
Timeliness expectations and common failure points
Assessing narrative versus quantitative disclosure
The role of auditors and gatekeepers
Group exercise: review a sample issuer disclosure against the full/accurate/timely standard
Common red flags in issuer disclosure
Linking disclosure weaknesses to wider governance or business model risk
Supervisory tools for challenging inadequate disclosure
Case study: a disclosure red flag scenario
Case study: analyse an issuer's disclosure and produce a supervisory assessment
Recap: disclosure as protection, quality assessment, red flags
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Financial Inclusion and Access to Services
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to introduce participants to financial inclusion as a policy and supervisory concern, exploring the barriers that prevent access to financial services and the regulatory tools available to promote inclusive access without compromising other…
objectives: Explain the concept and measurement of financial inclusion
Identify common barriers to accessing financial services
Discuss the tension between financial inclusion and financial crime controls
Evaluate inclusive product design practices
Assess the role of regulation in promoting or hindering inclusion
Identify policy options to improve financial inclusion outcomes
syllabus: Defining and measuring financial inclusion
Barriers: cost, access, documentation, trust, digital literacy
Financial inclusion as a supervisory and policy concern
Global perspectives on inclusion initiatives
Facilitated discussion: barriers to access in participants' own markets
The 'de-risking' problem: how AML/CFT controls can restrict access
Balancing proportionate financial crime controls with inclusion
Inclusive product design: simplified accounts, tiered KYC
International examples of proportionate approaches
Group discussion: designing a proportionate KYC regime for a basic account product
The supervisor's role in promoting inclusion
Policy levers: proportionality, guidance, innovation hubs
Measuring progress on financial inclusion
Case study: an inclusion initiative and its outcomes
Case study exercise: assess an inclusion initiative and propose improvements
Recap: barriers, tensions, policy options
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Consumer Outcomes Monitoring and Supervisory Judgement
modules.summary: How to use firm data, complaints, market intelligence and thematic work to identify poor consumer outcomes, prioritise follow-up and communicate findings to firms.
objectives: Identify indicators of poor consumer outcomes in firm and market data
Prioritise supervisory follow-up proportionately
Communicate findings and required remediation to firms
syllabus: Outcome indicators: claims, cancellations, persistency and switching
Thematic reviews, mystery shopping and consumer research
Linking weak controls to wider conduct risk
Remediation, redress exercises and enforcement referral

modules.title: Emerging Consumer Harms and the Authority's Response
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining new sources of consumer harm, from digital distribution to AI-driven pricing, and building the authority's consumer protection plan.
objectives: Anticipate consumer harms from digital and AI-driven business models
Evaluate the authority's consumer protection tools and gaps
Produce a prioritised consumer protection action plan
syllabus: Digital distribution, buy-now-pay-later and finfluencers
AI-driven pricing, personalisation and fairness
Scams, fraud and the shifting boundary of firm responsibility
Workshop: the authority's consumer protection priorities

related.title: Conduct, Culture and Behavioural Supervision
related.summary: An eight-module programme on assessing conduct risk and culture in firms, using behavioural insights, data and targeted supervisory interventions.

related.title: Cross-Border and Group Supervision
related.summary: An eight-module programme on home-host supervision, consolidated group oversight, MoUs, supervisory colleges, third-country firms and cross-border crisis cooperation.

related.title: FinTech Business Models: Understanding and Supervising Innovation
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and firm compliance teams to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their risks.
